strengths: Extends the optimistic MLE / observable-operator-model framework from single-agent weakly-revealing POMDPs to the more general and less-studied setting of POMGs against adaptive (strategic) adversaries, combining two previously separate research threads (policy regret and partially observable RL) in a technically nontrivial way.

The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.7) separating the world-channel operator from the adversary-aggregation operator is a clean and useful structural insight that cleanly isolates where partial observability and adversary adaptivity each enter the analysis, and the proof is carried out carefully with explicit augmented-state constructions.

The paper provides both an upper bound (via an epoch-based, one-policy-per-epoch optimistic MLE algorithm) and a lower bound, and explicitly explains the key algorithmic design choice (geometrically growing epochs) that keeps the posterior-Lipschitz "transport cost" logarithmic rather than polynomial in T, with a clear, intuitive explanation of why naive batching would yield only T^{3/4} regret.

Useful set of extensions (horizon adaptivity, fading-memory adversaries, tabular instantiation) that show the core algorithm and analysis are reasonably robust/generalizable without requiring redesign.

The posterior-Lipschitz condition is defined via a fixed reference measure to avoid a circularity problem the authors identify in related concurrent work, which is a legitimate and well-explained methodological fix if the concern is valid.
weaknesses: The matching lower bound (Theorem 4.1) is proven only for a degenerate instance (H=2, fully revealing, memoryless adversary with L=0, essentially a stochastic bandit problem), so it only certifies the sqrt(T) and sqrt(d_E) dependence at leading order. It does not validate the more distinctive and technically involved parts of the upper bound — the H and m dependence, the posterior-Lipschitz transport cost, or the specific role of partial observability/adversary memory in the aggregate Eluder dimension — leaving a considerable gap between the sophistication of the upper-bound machinery and what is actually shown to be unavoidable. The paper's own title ("Minimax-Optimal") somewhat overstates what is established.

The algorithm is a purely oracle-based/statistical construction (exact MLE and optimistic planning oracles over Ξ), and the paper explicitly acknowledges that planning is PSPACE-complete and confidence-set optimization intractable in general; no computationally efficient algorithm or approximation is given even for the tabular case, substantially limiting practical significance despite the motivating examples (autonomous driving, trading, cybersecurity) suggesting real-world relevance.

The result rests on a large stack of nontrivial assumptions (posterior-Lipschitz adversary, multi-step weak revealing, and six-part statistical regularity conditions including exact warm-up stationarity with 'no residual transient' and uniformly bounded log-likelihood ratios requiring positivity/smoothing). While individually each is described as standard, their conjunction is demanding, and Assumption 3.1(vi) (exact stationarity after finite warm-up) is a strong idealization that may not hold for realistic adaptive adversaries, especially outside the fading-memory extension.

No empirical validation or simulation is provided, even a small synthetic example, to sanity-check the derived rates, the role of the aggregate Eluder dimension, or the practical impact of the epoch-based versus batch-based schedule.

There remain acknowledged looseness/gaps in the analysis itself (e.g., Remarks C.9–C.10 note that the stated bound is not the tightest possible depending on which KL-to-operator conversion or Eluder class is used), indicating the presented rate, while sqrt(T), is not fully tight in its other parameters (H, m) even relative to the paper's own analysis.

Appendix H contains an unusually extensive, lemma-by-lemma technical takedown of a concurrent/contemporaneous submission (identified by name and OpenReview link as an ICLR submission), reproducing and critiquing its internal equations and lemma numbers in detail; this raises questions about how the authors obtained such detailed knowledge of an unpublished concurrent submission and is atypical practice that referees should scrutinize for potential ethical/confidentiality concerns.

The overall contribution, once the reference-measure fix and epoch-vs-batch modification are set aside, is an incremental generalization/refinement of very closely related recent work (Nguyen-Tang & Arora 2024/2025; Liu et al. 2022a/2023; the cited concurrent POMG paper), and the paper could more clearly delineate which parts of the analysis are genuinely new versus adaptations of existing techniques.

strengths: Careful resolution of a real circularity issue in defining posterior-Lipschitz adversaries via a fixed reference-measure construction, improving on a concurrent formulation.

Elegant causal decomposition of the observable operator into world-channel and adversary-aggregation components (Theorem 2.5), cleanly separating θ- and Φ-dependence and enabling separate Eluder-dimension analysis per channel.
Necessity of the statistical termination test is proved rather than asserted (Proposition D.5), showing Ω(T) regret for a fixed-schedule variant on a valid instance.
A matching Ω(√dET) lower bound is given, with the paper transparently noting which dependencies (H, m, κ, L) remain unresolved rather than overclaiming full optimality.

Multiple extensions (horizon-adaptivity, fading-memory adversaries, tabular rates) are worked out with full proofs, and a quantitative, explicit comparison against concurrent work identifies a specific T^{3/4} obstruction in an alternative flat-batching approach.
Includes empirical validation, including a check of the termination test's necessity and scaling experiments, unusual and welcome for a primarily theoretical contribution.
weaknesses: The core techniques (optimistic MLE, epoch-based termination, Eluder summability) are largely adapted from prior POMDP/Markov-game policy-regret work rather than fundamentally new; the main novel content is the causal decomposition and adversary-class formalization.

The layered assumption structure (posterior-Lipschitz adversary, multi-step weak revealing, five-part statistical regularity) is heavy and its practical scope is illustrated by few concrete natural examples, making it hard to judge real restrictiveness.

The lower bound only establishes optimality in T and the aggregate Eluder dimension, using a trivial memoryless fully-revealing instance; optimality in H, m, κ, and the Lipschitz constant L is left open, so the 'minimax-optimal' title claim is stronger than what is proven.
Computational tractability is essentially unaddressed: optimistic planning is PSPACE-hard in general, and the proposed posterior-sampling alternative is unanalyzed, limiting practical applicability.

Empirical validation is restricted to closed-form tractable bandit-embedded instances and a small heuristic classification task that does not actually instantiate the general optimistic-MLE algorithm on a genuine POMG.

A large appendix is devoted to critiquing a concurrent, apparently not-yet-peer-reviewed submission; while mathematically detailed, this comparison is based solely on the authors' own re-derivation and is unusually central to the paper's claimed advantage.

Eluder dimension bounds require a restrictive 'coordinate-structured' parameterization (excluding bilinear/factored models), and even the tractable tabular/linear instantiations carry large polynomial dependence on |S|, |A|, |B|, |OA|^κ, |OB|^κ, limiting practical significance.

strengths: Provides a comprehensive theoretical treatment of a genuinely difficult and underexplored problem: policy regret minimization under both partial observability and adaptive/strategic adversaries. The paper delivers a matching upper and lower bound (Theorems 3.3 and 4.1), establishing minimax optimality in T and the aggregate Eluder dimension, which is a strong and rare combination for this level of model complexity.

The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.5) separating the observable operator into a world channel and an adversary-aggregation channel is a clean and technically substantive contribution that enables tracking Eluder complexity separately for each source of uncertainty, and is reused effectively throughout the analysis (e.g., channel-triangle inequalities).

The necessity of data-dependent statistical termination is not just asserted but rigorously proven (Proposition D.5), with an explicit construction showing that fixed epoch schedules incur linear regret under valid tie-breaking. This is a nice, falsifiable structural insight that strengthens the paper's algorithmic design choices.

Careful and detailed technical comparison with concurrent work (Sang & Nguyen-Tang, 2025), identifying a specific circularity issue in their posterior-Lipschitz formulation and quantifying how their flat-batching schedule leads to a T^{3/4}-scale transport term, explaining precisely why the one-policy-per-epoch design with cumulative confidence sets avoids this obstruction.

The paper is unusually thorough for a theory paper: it includes horizon-adaptive guarantees, fading-memory extensions, explicit tabular instantiation, and even an empirical validation section testing the theoretical predictions (necessity of termination, scaling laws, and behavior on a semi-realistic adaptive-adversary task), lending credibility to the abstract guarantees.
weaknesses: The manuscript is extremely dense with many layered assumptions (posterior-Lipschitz, multi-step weak revealing, statistical regularity with several sub-conditions), and it can be difficult to assess how restrictive the combination of these conditions is in practice or how they interact; some readers may struggle to build intuition despite the extended proof sketch.

Computational tractability is explicitly out of scope (Section 5.4): optimistic planning is PSPACE-complete in general and confidence-set optimization compounds this, so the statistical guarantees, while sharp, do not translate into a practical algorithm for anything beyond small tabular/structured instances.

The lower bound (Theorem 4.1) only establishes optimality in T and the aggregate Eluder dimension; the paper explicitly does not close the gap on the H and m dependence, leaving open how tight the horizon and memory factors in the upper bound actually are.

Empirical validation, while a nice addition, is limited in scale (bandit-embedded POMGs and a small digit-classification simulation with a hand-designed adversary) and necessarily uses a simulated adversary since real strategic-response data does not exist in logged form; this limits how much the experiments can validate the theory beyond the constructed worst-case instances.

Many constants in the bounds are hidden inside O~ notation and depend on multiple problem parameters (e.g., B0, cKL, ακ) in ways that are not always made fully explicit, which could make it harder for practitioners to gauge the real magnitude of the guarantees.
